planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Virginia bugleweed spreads by slender stolons that tip off into small overwintering tubers, a trait historically noted when the tubers were gathered as an emergency food source.

directions: This eastern North American wetland mint is the species most classically referenced as 'Bugleweed' in nineteenth-century Eclectic and modern herbal medicine, used much like its close relatives L. americanus and L. europaeus to calm an overactive thyroid, though it is a distinct species recognizable by its slender stolons that swell into small tubers at the tips. Plant it in permanently moist, humus-rich soil at a pond edge, rain garden, or shaded stream bank, where it spreads gradually to form a low colony. Small white flowers cluster tightly in the leaf axils in summer and draw small native bees, though the plant is grown primarily for its medicinal and naturalizing value rather than showy bloom. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to control spread and share plants.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed outdoors in autumn into permanently damp, peaty, slightly acid to neutral fen soil, since this umbellifer needs a period of cold, moist stratification and germinates erratically from stored seed.

directions: Milk parsley takes its common name from the milky latex that oozes from a cut stem, a useful field mark separating it from similar wetland umbellifers. It is a monocarpic perennial of European fens and calcareous wet meadows, forming a rosette of finely divided, carrot-like leaves for one or more seasons before sending up flat umbels of small white flowers on a tall hollow stem. The species is best known as the sole larval food plant of the British swallowtail butterfly subspecies in the Norfolk Broads, making it a valuable addition to a constructed fen garden or wildlife wetland planting. Grow in permanently saturated, peaty, nutrient-poor fen conditions and avoid drying out the root zone, which this species will not tolerate for long.

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings or plant nursery divisions in spring into lean, sharply drained, limy scree or trough mix in full sun; this limestone-cliff endemic rots quickly in rich or poorly drained garden soil.

directions: Endemic to limestone cliffs and rocky gorges of the Dinaric Alps in Croatia and neighboring Balkan coastal mountains, this diminutive aromatic subshrub forms a tight, woody-based cushion of small gray-green leaves studded in summer with whorls of pale pink to lilac tubular flowers that bees visit readily. It is a natural fit for a sunny scree bed, limestone trough, or dry rock garden wall where its need for sharp drainage and lean soil can be met. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the cushion dense and prevent the base from becoming woody and open. Established plants tolerate considerable summer drought but will not survive standing winter moisture around the crown.

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in cool weather; unlike its fragrant relative Reseda odorata, this species tolerates light transplanting from small pots if direct sowing isn't possible.

directions: White mignonette is a taller, more upright Mediterranean relative of common fragrant mignonette, grown chiefly for its dense, architectural spikes of small white flowers rather than for scent, which is much fainter than Reseda odorata. It thrives in cool weather and fertile, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil, bolting and declining once summer heat sets in, so treat it as a cool-season annual for spring and autumn borders. The stiff flowering spikes make a good filler for cut-flower bouquets and hold up well once cut. It has naturalized along roadsides and waste ground in parts of the western United States and the Mediterranean basin, where it readily self-sows in disturbed, sunny sites.

planting.note: Direct-sow or set out transplants after the last frost into full sun and average, well-drained soil; grown as a frost-killed warm-season annual outside its hardy subtropical range.

directions: Siberian motherwort carries showier pink-purple whorled flower spikes than its European and Chinese relatives, making it as much a pollinator-garden ornamental as a medicinal herb; bees work the blooms heavily, giving rise to the common name honeyweed in parts of its naturalized range. Despite the name, it is native to parts of Asia and has become a widespread warm-climate weed and traditional herb throughout Latin America and Southeast Asia, where the dried flowering tops are brewed for fevers and digestive complaints. Direct-sow after frost danger passes into full sun and ordinary garden soil; the plant grows quickly, flowers over a long season, and self-sows readily where winters are mild. Avoid use during pregnancy, as with other Leonurus species, due to traditional reports of uterine-stimulant activity.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; like other Mediterranean Ballota species it needs dry winter footing far more than it needs mild temperatures.

directions: Native to rocky hillsides of Crete and the southern Aegean, Cretan horehound is grown chiefly for its persistent, cup-shaped, papery pale green-pink calyces that follow the small summer flowers and dry beautifully on the stem, earning the plant the nickname smoke bells among dried-flower growers. The felted, scalloped, silver-gray leaves give year-round textural interest in a dry Mediterranean border or gravel garden, even between flowering seasons. Grow in lean, sharply drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, and withhold supplemental water once established except during extended drought. Cut stems for drying just as the calyces mature and before they begin to shatter, and shear the plant lightly afterward to maintain a compact habit and prevent a woody, gappy center.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online
